Okay, I’ve just reconfigured the server and client code to use port 4747 instead of the default 3000. The edits to server.js, src/net.js, and the test script were successful, and I verified that ports 4000, 4200, and 4747 are currently free. However, the earlier attempt to run the smoke test failed because the WebSocket client received an HTTP 200 response, which turned out to be due to Docker’s WSL relay also listening on port 3000 and, more importantly, a lingering Node process that was still bound to that port from a previous run of the server.

When I checked the active listeners on port 3000, the output showed three processes: `wslrelay pid=10424`, `com.docker.backend pid=6636`, and `node pid=49356`. The Docker-related processes are expected to stay; they’re just part of the environment and don’t interfere with my server now that I’m moving to a different port. The Node process, however, is the old instance of my multiplayer server that was started earlier (the “KILLHOUSE server running” line in the background task output). That process is still alive and holding onto port 3000, which could cause confusion or accidental connections if anything else tries to use the default port.

Since I’ve already changed the code to listen on 4747, the next logical step is to stop that stale Node process so it no longer occupies port 3000. This will clean up the environment and ensure that when I later start the server again (presumably on the new port), there won’t be any leftover processes interfering. I don’t need to stop the Docker or WSL relay processes; they’re unrelated to my application.

Therefore, I’ll issue a PowerShell command to force‑kill the Node process with PID 49356, suppress any confirmation prompts, and then pause briefly to give the OS time to release the port. This sets the stage for a fresh start of the server on the new port.
